turns.script: What's the difference between a process and a thread?
turns.asr_text: What's the difference between a process and a thread?

turns.text_generated:
Oh, this is a fun one! Okay, picture it like this: a process is like a whole house, with its own rooms, furniture, and everything inside. It’s got its own memory space, resources, and it runs independently.

Now, a thread is like a person inside that house, doing a specific task. Multiple threads can live in the same house (process), and they share the same resources, like memory. But they can do different tasks all at once, working together.

So, in short: a process is the big container, and threads are the individual workers inside that container. Processes don’t share memory with each other, but threads within the same process do share memory. That means threads can be faster and more lightweight, while processes are more isolated and robust.

turns.script: Okay, so which one is cheaper to create?
turns.asr_text: Okay, so which one is cheaper to create?

turns.text_generated: Threads are generally cheaper to create than processes. Why? Because a thread uses the existing memory space and resources of its parent process, so it doesn’t have to set up a whole new environment. It’s like adding another person to a house, rather than building a completely new house from scratch. Creating a process involves allocating its own separate memory space, loading new resources, and establishing its own environment, which takes more time and overhead. So, in a nutshell, threads are lighter, faster, and cheaper to spin up compared to processes.

turns.text_generated:
Ah, great question! So, here’s why: when you create a process, the operating system has to do a lot of heavy lifting. It allocates a whole new memory space, sets up its own system resources, file descriptors, environment variables—basically, it’s building an entirely new playground from zero. This takes time and system resources. 

Threads, on the other hand, live inside an existing process, so they share the same memory space, the same code, and a lot of the same resources. All the OS has to do is set up a new execution context, like a separate register set, a stack, and boom—it’s ready to run. 

So, threads are cheaper because they’re just adding new workers inside an already built process, rather than starting from scratch.
